essentials: REACH is the EU's **general chemicals law**. It applies to substances on their own, in mixtures and in finished products, which it calls articles.
For product companies two parts matter most: the **restrictions** in Annex XVII and the **information duties** for substances of very high concern.
If an article contains a substance from the **Candidate List above 0.1% by weight**, customers must be told and the article must be notified to the SCIP database.
The **EU importer** is responsible for what is in imported goods.

sections.title: Why it exists
text: Before REACH, most chemicals on the market had never been assessed, and authorities had to prove a substance was dangerous before they could act. REACH reversed the burden: companies must show that the substances they make or import can be used safely. The principle is ‘no data, no market’.

sections.title: The four processes
points: **Registration**: manufacturers and importers of a substance in quantities of one tonne or more per year submit data on its properties and uses to the European Chemicals Agency, ECHA.
**Evaluation**: ECHA and Member States check the registrations and selected substances.
**Authorisation**: substances of very high concern listed in Annex XIV may only be used with a specific authorisation after a sunset date.
**Restriction**: Annex XVII bans or limits substances in defined uses, including in articles. This is the part that works like RoHS.

sections.title: Substances of very high concern in articles
text: Substances that cause cancer, damage fertility, disrupt hormones or persist in the environment can be identified as substances of very high concern and put on the **Candidate List**. The list is updated twice a year. From the day a substance is listed, suppliers of articles have duties:
points: **Tell business customers** (Article 33): pass on the name of the substance and information for safe use, with the delivery.
**Answer consumers** within 45 days, free of charge, when they ask.
**Notify the SCIP database** at ECHA, so that waste operators know where such substances are.
**Notify ECHA** (Article 7) if the total amount in all articles exceeds one tonne per year, unless the use is already registered.
after: The 0.1% threshold applies to each article in the legal sense, including every component that was an article before assembly: ‘once an article, always an article’. A handle containing a listed plasticiser triggers the duty even if it is a small part of the tool.

sections.title: Restrictions that matter for tools
points: **PAHs** in rubber and plastic parts that touch the skin, such as grips.
**Lead** and **cadmium** in various articles, plastics and coatings.
**Nickel** release from parts in prolonged skin contact.
A **broad PFAS restriction** covering thousands of substances is being assessed. PFAS are used in seals, lubricants, coatings and battery components.

sections.title: Who is responsible
text: A manufacturer outside the EU has no duties under REACH. They fall on whoever brings the goods into the EU: the **importer**. A non-EU producer can appoint an **only representative** to register substances, which relieves importers of that task, but the article duties stay with the importer and each supplier down the chain. Enforcement and penalties are national.

terms.text: An object whose shape, surface or design determines its function more than its chemical composition. A tool, a screw and a cable are articles.

The list of restrictions on manufacture, placing on the market and use.

An EU entity appointed by a non-EU manufacturer to fulfil the registration duties of importers.

mistakes.right: Every importer and supplier of articles has duties, in particular for Candidate List substances and restrictions.

mistakes.wrong: 0.1% is calculated on the whole product.
mistakes.right: It is calculated for each component article.

mistakes.wrong: A declaration from last year is still valid.
mistakes.right: The Candidate List changes twice a year. A declaration is only as current as the list it was checked against.

mistakes.wrong: A Candidate List substance may not be used.
mistakes.right: Listing triggers information duties. A ban follows only through authorisation or restriction.

practice: **Collect declarations per article** against the current Candidate List and Annex XVII.
**Refresh them after each list update**; build the request into supplier contracts.
**Test risk parts**: grips, cables, seals, coated and coloured parts.
**Prepare customer information and SCIP notifications** for articles above 0.1%.
**Screen for PFAS** now, so that you know where substitution would be needed.

quiz.q: A tool's rubber grip contains a Candidate List substance at 0.3% of the grip's weight, but far less than 0.1% of the whole tool. Do the information duties apply?
options: No, the whole tool is the reference
Yes, the threshold applies to each component article
Only if the tool is sold to children
Only above one tonne per year
quiz.why: Every component that was an article before assembly is assessed on its own.

quiz.q: Who is responsible under REACH for a tool made outside the EU?
quiz.why: REACH duties fall on EU actors. For imported articles that is the importer, and every supplier further down the chain for the information duties.

quiz.q: How long does a supplier have to answer a consumer's question about Candidate List substances in an article?
quiz.why: The information must be provided free of charge within 45 days.

quiz.q: What does inclusion in the Candidate List mean?
options: Information duties apply at once; a ban may follow later
The substance must be registered again
quiz.why: Listing triggers the article duties immediately. Use is only restricted through Annex XIV or Annex XVII.

quiz.q: Which part of REACH bans or limits substances in defined uses, similar to RoHS?
quiz.why: Annex XVII contains the restrictions, such as on PAHs in grips.

quiz.q: How often is the Candidate List usually updated?
quiz.why: New substances are typically added twice a year, which is why supplier declarations need regular renewal.
